questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the point of inflection on $y = x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 9x + 2$.

options.why: Solved $6x + 6 = 0$ as $x = 1$, dropping the negative sign, then substituted $x = 1$.
Solved $6x + 6 = 0$ correctly but substituted $x = 1$ into the original function.
Solved $6x + 6 = 0$ as $x = 1$ but substituted $x = -1$ into the original function.

questions.question_text: Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection on $y = x^{4} - 4x^{3} + 18x$.

options.why: Solved $12x(x - 2) = 0$ and kept only the root from the first factor.
Divided both sides of $12x^{2} - 24x = 0$ by $12x$, losing the root $x = 0$.
Took the midpoint of the two roots of $y''$, as though a quartic had a single inflection like a cubic.

questions.solution_text:
$y' = 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 18$
$y'' = 12x^{2} - 24x$
$= 12x(x - 2)$
So $y'' = 0$ when $x = 0$ or $x = 2$.
At $x = -1$, $y'' = 36 > 0$; at $x = 1$, $y'' = -12 < 0$; at $x = 3$, $y'' = 36 > 0$.
The concavity changes at both values, so both are points of inflection.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = x^{6}$ has $y'' = 30x^{4}$, so $y''(0) = 0$. What happens at the origin?

options.text: There is no point of inflection; the origin is a local minimum turning point.
There is a horizontal point of inflection, because $y'(0) = 0$ and $y''(0) = 0$.
options.why: Solved $y'' = 0$ and stopped, without testing whether the concavity actually changes.

options.text: There is a point of inflection with a non-zero gradient.
options.why: Assumed every solution of $y'' = 0$ is an inflection, and also overlooked that $y'(0) = 0$.

options.text: There is a local maximum turning point.
options.why: Read the even power as producing a curve that opens downwards.

questions.solution_text:
$y'' = 30x^{4}$
$y''(-1) = 30 > 0$
$y''(1) = 30 > 0$
The second derivative is positive on both sides, so the concavity does not change and there is no point of inflection.
$y' = 6x^{5}$, so $y'(-1) = -6 < 0$ and $y'(1) = 6 > 0$.
The gradient changes from negative to positive, so the origin is a local minimum turning point.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = 2x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 6x + 1$ has a point of inflection at $x = 1$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a horizontal point of inflection at $(1, 3)$.
It is a point of inflection at $(1, 3)$ with gradient $6$.
options.why: Evaluated $y'$ at $x = 0$ rather than at $x = 1$.

options.text: It is a horizontal point of inflection at $(1, 1)$.
options.why: Read the constant term $1$ as the $y$-coordinate instead of substituting $x = 1$ into the function.

options.text: It is a local minimum turning point at $(1, 3)$.
options.why: Saw $y'(1) = 0$ and assumed a stationary point must be a turning point.

questions.solution_text:
$y' = 6x^{2} - 12x + 6$
$= 6(x - 1)^{2}$
$y'(1) = 0$, so the tangent at the inflection is horizontal.
$y(1) = 2 - 6 + 6 + 1 = 3$
There is a horizontal point of inflection at $(1, 3)$.

questions.question_text: A function has second derivative $f''(x) = (x + 1)^{2}(x - 4)$. At which values of $x$ does the curve have points of inflection?

options.why: Took every root of $f''(x) = 0$ as an inflection without testing for a change of sign.
Chose the repeated root, assuming the squared factor is what marks the change of concavity.

options.text: There are none, because $f''(x)$ is never zero.
options.why: Read $(x + 1)^{2}$ as strictly positive and concluded the whole product can never be zero.

questions.solution_text:
$f''(x) = 0$ when $x = -1$ or $x = 4$.
$f''(-2) = (1)(-6) = -6 < 0$
$f''(0) = (1)(-4) = -4 < 0$
The sign does not change at $x = -1$, so it is not a point of inflection.
$f''(3) = (16)(-1) = -16 < 0$
$f''(5) = (36)(1) = 36 > 0$
The sign changes at $x = 4$, so that is the only point of inflection.

questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the point of inflection on $y = xe^{-x}$.

options.why: Solved $y' = 0$ instead of $y'' = 0$, which gives the stationary point rather than the inflection.
Solved $x - 2 = 0$ as $x = -2$, reading the factor backwards.
Found $x = 2$ correctly but substituted into $e^{x}$ rather than $e^{-x}$.

questions.solution_text:
$y' = e^{-x} - xe^{-x}$
$= e^{-x}(1 - x)$
$y'' = -e^{-x}(1 - x) - e^{-x}$
$= e^{-x}(x - 2)$
Since $e^{-x} > 0$, set $x - 2 = 0$.
$x = 2$
At $x = 1$, $y'' = -e^{-1} < 0$; at $x = 3$, $y'' = e^{-3} > 0$, so the concavity changes.
$y(2) = 2e^{-2}$
The point of inflection is $\left(2, \dfrac{2}{e^{2}}\right)$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = 3\sin x + x$ has second derivative $y'' = -3\sin x$. Find its point of inflection for $0 < x < 2\pi$.

options.why: Substituted into $3\sin x$ only and left out the $+x$ term when finding the $y$-coordinate.
Took a solution of $\sin x = 0$ that lies outside the open domain $0 < x < 2\pi$.
Took the other solution of $\sin x = 0$ that lies outside the open domain $0 < x < 2\pi$.

questions.solution_text:
Set $y'' = 0$:
$-3\sin x = 0$
$\sin x = 0$
The only solution with $0 < x < 2\pi$ is $x = \pi$.
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y'' = -3 < 0$; at $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, $y'' = 3 > 0$, so the concavity changes.
$y(\pi) = 3\sin\pi + \pi = \pi$
The point of inflection is $(\pi, \pi)$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = x^{3} + bx^{2} + 5x - 1$ has a point of inflection at $x = -2$. What is the value of $b$?

options.why: Solved $-12 + 2b = 0$ as $2b = -12$, keeping the sign of $6x$ on the wrong side.
Reached $2b = 12$ but did not divide by $2$.
Both moved $-12$ across without changing its sign and did not divide by $2$.
